I thought about restarting but the gameplay loop feels almost painful with how little progress you make everyday. I also can help with like 15 quests available that week and getting all that done can be a lot, I know I don't have to do quests but progress is basically built on the quest system to get random recipes. I also feel like farming is not really that suitable for this game but it's understandable as something people did but man you really struggle to make enough to eat and survive. Other games offer ways to make it less time consuming  but I feel there aren't a lot of options in this game. I'm up-voting in the hopes the dev can add more marriage toggles and options, though not sure how that will go. Also adding visuals to the fishing mini game suggesting the key direction would go a long way, I was very confused on that mini game for a while. I guess overall it feels sluggish to me game wise. I'll likely restart my file and maybe just turn off disease for now but preventing some marriages might have at least left me with more options earlier. The random chance for progression also makes it feel slow too.

I don't.... [i]dislike[/i] the game... but I also can't really say I'm a huge fan of it. I'm giving it a positive because it has potential, but with how all the mechanics work, it's hard to really feel invested or motivated to do much of anything in this game.

Why bother getting to know villagers or marry them if they're just going to die and they pretty much all have the same personality? Sure, it's required to continue because your original character can die and you need someone to replace them, but then.... how do I go about caring about building a family in this game? 

I ran into the same problem with Kynseed's characters. The story and environments made that game worth playing for alone (this game doesn't really feel like it has that factor going for it yet), but the characters were all stale and not worth interacting with beyond the need to marry so that you could continue the game through your bloodline.

I just don't think I really see the point. There's potential here, but for someone like me who likes established characters to relate to and enjoy reading on and interacting with, it's hard to really see the point to anything in this game. 

Maybe playing it some more will change that for me.

I'm obsessed with the cozy game genre, and love keeping up with the new offerings. Creating a game with a running lineage and history that you can connect with over a long term is such a fun and excellent addition to the genre, and this game shows an excellent amount of promise for future development. 

Good: The graphics are simple and well executed, and create an absolutely charming aesthetic. The animation is fun, and for what is largely just 2D vector sprites, the world is surprisingly immersive and rich with detail. The gameplay is effective and engaging, and the game offers you a considerable amount of freedom with how you approach your town's story, creating a very "sims-like" environment.

Bad: Poorly refined control timing can make you feel like the game is resisting you, and can be all the difference between a game feeling grindy, and a game feeling engaging and addictive. In this game, I feel like it falls on the grindy side of its actions. The hitboxes on items you click to pick up could be slightly bigger, and a whole handful of gripes I could list, but none of which (aside from pacing) significantly detract from the experience. 

Over all, I think this game is going to be a fun one to see evolve over time. I'm engaged and eager to play more, and would recommend it for game enthusiasts who love to see a solid work of passion grow over time. The fact that it was made by two developers is astounding.

Cutesy Colonialism-era Paper Mario-like aesthetics, otherwise it's Stardew Valley for realists: Food spoils.  Tools break.  People die of old age and disease.  Even your main character, whose gameplay continues through their children after death, Kynseed style.  Well, it's not realistic in all ways.  Witch magic works, and not a single clergyman around to burn them at the stake, because this setting satisfies all the political expectations of our time.  And yet, you can opt to bump off your fellow colonists if they rub you the wrong way, so despite the cozy, politically correct trappings of this colonial-era farming/life sim game, there's an edge to it.

The developers walk a fine line, but I dig what they're trying to do here.  I like Animal Crossing, but it kind of peters out into an endless furniture-collection and portrait collection game where you go nowhere.  I like the average Farming Sim RPG genre (Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons/Stardew Valley and its ilk) but there's often a static world, none of the familiar faces ever change, even if you can upgrade your homestead and the town.  So I was excited that Echoes of the Plum Grove was taking things a little further, and it delivers increased consequence.

That said, I would prefer they had gone further yet.  Intrigues among the NPCs don't go anywhere near what a player is capable of.  At most, some NPCs will be chronically grumpy or occasionally sad, they'll spread disease around, and they'll marry your crushes or pop their clogs when you don't want them to.  But that's about it, and you can expect whoever fills their shoes to be a fairly indistinct replacement to whomever was lost.  Given the setting, perhaps a proper Werewolf/Mafia-style game was in the cards at some point in development, but I haven't seen it yet.  I would have liked to be a sleuth but, instead, I'm just a settler trying to secure the bloodline before the reaper catches me.

Still, heartily recommended.  It's not a very expensive game, chances are it'll be good for at least 20 hours in its present state, and who knows what future updates will bring?

For a dev group of 2, the game shines! I'm always on the look out for a. Farming/Homesteading sims and b. Unique art style

Echoes of the Plum Grove covers both of those bases and then some. There are some aspects of the game that weren't advertised and I was very pleasantly surprised of! No spoilers of course. ;) I also very much like the idea that it takes place in the colonial era and you're just trying to get by.

There are some QoL aspects that I would like to see implemented in future updates (the devs are planning more updates) that would make this game sparkle:

- inventory sorting and chest sorting: as of writing this, there is no way to auto sort your inventory and chests. If you put away an item that already has a stack in a chest, it will not automatically stack. Instead it will occupy an empty space in the chest.

- sprint ability: while you will unlock the means to move faster rather early on in the game, it's a temporary consumable and the ingredients are hard to come by early on. Not to mention the means to craft it is on the other side of town. While there is fast traveling, it still consumes day time, which already passes rather quickly anyways.

- crafting at shops: until you get a random quest with the recipe or unlock with leveling up, you cannot create artisan goods or smelt. While there is a perfectly good forge available in town, you cannot use it, leaving you to pay a rather large sum of money (and time since NPCs stock may only have 1 or 2 available for the day) for nails and bars until you can craft one yourself. The forge, along with other artisan machines that are in town, could be available to use if the shop is open, if the player pays a small fee, or if their friendship is high enough with one of the shop owners. 

While I have other nit picky thoughts, they're just nit picky and don't affect the quality of the game in its entirety. The devs are clearly hard workers, their love for this project is very apparent, so I don't want my complaints to be detrimental  to anybody purchasing it. It's cute, fun, cozy, whimsical. Please do it give it a try! It's worth the $20.

Let me open my review by stating I love cozy games, but farming sims are really hit or miss for me. I, like many others, were drawn in by the Cozy Gamers FB group and their free marketing. The game looked chaotic to me, and I wanted to give it a try because it seemed like most of the fun was in how volatile the day to day gameplay could be. So I downloaded it and gave it a try. 

Imagine my surprise and delight when I could simply turn off all the things that stressed me out about farming sims. No energy meter, no item and tool degradation, and although I did try to keep the hunger meter on, I found keeping up with it was stressful at the beginning of the game so I simply turned it off. With these settings toggled off I quickly found that this game is my dream farming sim! 

With no energy meter to hold me back, I found for the first time I actually farmed in a farming sim game. Without worrying about keeping resources on me to fix my tools I happily gathered resources to please my villagers and focus on picking a partner instead. I have just been having a blast! What makes it unique is the plagues that have the potential to wipe out your entire village. Although very tragic, it keeps me on my toes and it’s a new twist to add to the farming sim genre that can sometimes be repetitive.

I had a few issues along the way, all of which were addressed directly and in a timely manner on discord by a member of the dev team, which I am thankful for. The only thing I would change is I wish the character’s dialogue would reflect the events they attend.  For example, the immersion breaks for me when people at funerals are stating “the day is taking forever” and “where is my dragon fruit cake?” But, it’s not game breaking and I am still enjoying my time seeing my villagers create new families and going about their lives. 

If you’re looking for something different with a cute art style but is still cozy and can be low stress depending on the settings you choose, please give this game a try. It’s definitely worth the $20 price tag!

[h1] I ADORE this game, it's full of charm and soul. [/h1]
So now that we got the bias out of the way, the inspirations of this game is quite clear while not feeling like a clone of any of em'.

[h2] So what is this game? [/h2]

The best comparison I can make is; imagine playing a Sims 2 Rags to Riches challenge, sprinkle in farming and homesteading as a core mechanic, set in Colonial Williamsburg and you're very close.
[i] (the girls who get it, get it) [/i]
I love Stardew Valley, chances are you love SV too, but this is not Stardew Valley, and it's not trying to be either.

[h2] Who would love this game? [/h2]

The player who enjoy a slow pace, being rewarded for patience and note keeping.
Anyone who knows how to appreciate a work, crafted with love and care.
Passion and care seeps from every pore of this game.

[b] And if you ever had a passion for either, American Girl (especially Kirsten) or Anne of Green Gables
Then I FIRMLY believe you should at least give this game a shot. [/b]

[h2] Who would hate this game? [/h2]

Want a quick reward? Action and fast paced game play? probably not for you

You love farming games and your favorite part is picking a romance partner and the little cutscenes between you and the towns folk? 
then this game might leave you feeling disappointed or wanting more from the social aspect.

This game punishes you for not paying attention and being reckless.
The social mechanics are there, with some quite charming dialog to add, HOWEVER;
it plays out much more like a Sims franchise social situation, instead of a Baldur's Gate or even Stardew Valley.

[h2] For the Cozy or Disabled player. [/h2]
(or in general, don't want some or all the challenge this game provides)

[b] The accessibility / difficulty settings [/b] of this game are quite generous.
They can be turned On and Off at any time in the game.
I will list them below as they stand as of (29th of June 2024):

[b] Fishing Minigame:[/b] Timed, Un-Timed, Off. (Off = No minigame, however you can still fish)
[b] Aging:[/b] Fast, Normal, Slow, Off.
[b] Player Aging:[/b] On, Off.
[b] Taxes:[/b] On, Off.
[b] Hunger:[/b] On, Off.
[b] Energy:[/b] On, Off.
[b] Diseases:[/b] On, Only NPCs, Off. (there are nausea and vomiting in this game. turning this off, removes it)
[b] Tool Durability:[/b] On, Off.
[b] Item Decay:[/b] On, Off.


[h2] Controls and Keybinding: [/h2]

At this current time as I am writing this (29th of June 2024)
[b] The controller support is available but still lacking [/b], however this being worked on and hopefully improved by the next patch.

[b] At this point in time there are no Keybinding options [/b] built into the game, I hope this changes in the future.

Echoes of the Plum Grove is a game where so many curious things can happen, making it very exciting to play.

There are so many farming games out there that are similar, but still try to give it uniqueness.
Here we have a game that doesn't just spoil us with all the positive aspects of a cozy game.
While in lots of farming games, we might have to worry about stamina, in this one diseases can wipe out your town's population.
Not to worry, since even when people pass, there will be others ready to take their spot in the village.

Echoes of the Plum Grove brings us not just farming, but also the difficulty of dealing with diseases, struggling not to starve, romancing villagers, building our property, decorating our home, raising a family, participating in events, and one of the most important things, we get to pay our weekly taxes to the rich mayor...
Some of these things make it seemingly more hard to thrive in this world, but also more exciting.

The game offers the option to turn off certain things, for example, "hunger", but I wouldn't recommend that.
All these options are there to give the game its flavor, but it is still great that we have that option for those who seek a more relaxed experience.

The village events are truly well done! I am so used to half-baked events that don't give you the feeling that it is a special day, that I ended up surprised.
Seeing busy people walk around the decorated places and also tourists made it special to me.
Having a school in the village which the kids visit was also a very thoughtful thing to add.

Echoes of the Plum Grove of course also comes with a story to uncover, but I don't want to spoil it, so you better experience it yourself.

Echoes of the Plum Grove, developed by Unwound Games and published by indie.io, is a beautifully melancholic and surprisingly complex take on the farming and life-simulation genre. At first glance, it looks like another cozy countryside game about planting crops, befriending villagers, and enjoying quiet days in a small town. Yet beneath its soft, watercolor aesthetic lies a system of survival, legacy, and mortality that turns this gentle world into something far more meaningful. It begins with a shipwreck that strands your character on the shores of Honeywood, a rural island village surrounded by forests and fields. What starts as a simple story of rebuilding a life slowly evolves into a generational saga in which time passes, families grow, and the choices you make ripple through decades of village history. The result is a game that feels both intimate and enduring—a blend of comfort and consequence rarely seen in its genre.

The foundation of Echoes of the Plum Grove rests on its blend of traditional farming sim mechanics and life-management systems. Players plant crops, tend livestock, gather resources, cook meals, craft tools, and build relationships with the townsfolk. The daily rhythm feels familiar to fans of Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon, but Echoes adds layers of realism and tension. Seasons are not just visual changes—they dictate the rhythm of survival. Crops wither if planted at the wrong time, and food spoils if hoarded carelessly. Winter, in particular, is an unforgiving season that tests how well you’ve prepared; without sufficient stockpiles of firewood, preserved food, and warm clothing, your character and their family can grow sick or even die. These mechanics give the game a grounded, almost historical tone—it’s less about endless productivity and more about sustainable living in a community that feels genuinely alive.

The game’s most distinctive feature is its generational system. Unlike many life sims that freeze time or loop endlessly, Echoes of the Plum Grove allows your character to age, fall ill, and eventually pass away. When that time comes, you continue the story through your descendants, inheriting the land, the family home, and the reputation your ancestor built. This sense of continuity transforms small decisions into lasting ones: how you treat your neighbors, how you manage your finances, or how you nurture your children all echo forward through the years. If you ignore your fields or neglect relationships, your descendants may face harder beginnings. If you leave behind wealth, strong social ties, and good health, they inherit an easier life. This mechanic turns what could have been a simple farming simulator into something contemplative and almost existential, making you consider not just how to live well, but how to be remembered.

Honeywood itself is one of the most charming and well-realized settings in recent simulation games. The village is filled with distinct characters, each with their own routines, preferences, and temperaments. Some are warm and friendly; others are prickly, gossipy, or downright unpleasant. Relationships must be nurtured through conversation, gift-giving, and mutual respect, but Echoes doesn’t shy away from friction. You can just as easily insult or alienate villagers as you can befriend them, and some quests even encourage mischievous or morally questionable behavior. This social realism keeps the world dynamic—people respond to your behavior, and friendships, rivalries, and even grudges can persist across generations. It’s a rare example of a cozy game that acknowledges that small-town life isn’t always idyllic. There’s gossip, jealousy, and tension, but also warmth and humor in equal measure.

The art and sound design elevate the game’s emotional tone. Visually, Echoes of the Plum Grove has the look of a handcrafted storybook—lush green fields, soft pastels, and charmingly simple character models. The gentle lighting shifts with the seasons, and the animation carries a quiet rhythm that mirrors the passage of time. It’s not flashy, but it’s evocative, managing to make even mundane actions like chopping wood or walking through the snow feel atmospheric. The music is equally understated, a collection of melodic and pastoral themes that shift with the mood of the season. Birds chirp in spring, wind howls in winter, and soft piano notes accompany your daily routines. The result is a world that feels warm but not saccharine, contemplative without being somber—a tone perfectly suited to the game’s themes of growth and transience.

While the core experience is rewarding, Echoes of the Plum Grove is not without its flaws. The social systems, though ambitious, can feel underdeveloped. NPC dialogue is often repetitive, and some villagers lack depth beyond a few simple lines or predictable routines. The AI behavior can be inconsistent—characters sometimes stand still for entire days or fail to react meaningfully to your presence. The quest design also wavers between inspired and underwhelming; while some storylines carry emotional weight, others feel like filler or lack satisfying resolution. The pacing can occasionally drag, particularly when managing the minutiae of daily survival, such as tool maintenance and illness recovery. These rough edges don’t break the experience, but they do reveal the growing pains of a small development team aiming for a deeply systemic world.

Yet, even with its imperfections, there is a sincerity to Echoes of the Plum Grove that makes it memorable. It does not rely on endless grinding or artificial goals to sustain engagement; instead, it encourages you to find meaning in small victories. Seeing your crops survive the winter, watching your children grow into adults, or witnessing your family’s home stand for generations carries a sense of permanence that most simulation games never attempt. It’s a quiet reflection on how lives unfold—how hardship, kindness, and resilience shape not only the present but the future as well. There’s a bittersweet pleasure in watching time pass, in knowing that every moment of prosperity is fleeting, yet still worth savoring.

Echoes of the Plum Grove succeeds because it understands that comfort and melancholy can coexist. It offers the joy of tending a garden, the satisfaction of building a home, and the sorrow of watching time take it all away. Its charm lies not in perfection but in the authenticity of its world—the feeling that you’re part of a living, breathing cycle of beginnings and endings. For players who want more than escapism, who crave a farming sim that values emotion and consequence as much as routine, it delivers something rare: a world that feels both cozy and alive, where the passage of time is not just a mechanic, but the heart of the experience.

"Echoes of the Plum Grove", developed by Unwound Games, is an enchanting indie RPG that whisks players away to a serene yet mysterious village. Set in a world brimming with folklore, magic, and deep emotional undertones, the game offers an immersive narrative experience complemented by stunning visuals and engaging gameplay.

Pros:
- Breathtaking Visuals: Echoes of the Plum Grove features exquisite art that brings the game’s mystical world to life. The vibrant colors and meticulous detail in the environments and character designs create a visually captivating experience.
- Rich, Emotional Storyline: The game excels in storytelling that is seemlessly weaved into a typical farming adventure, weaving a compelling narrative filled with folklore, personal journeys, and emotional depth. The plot twists and character arcs keep players deeply invested in the unfolding drama.
- Immersive Atmosphere: The combination of evocative music, ambient sounds, and detailed environments crafts an atmospheric experience that draws players into the heart of the village and its surrounding mysteries.

Cons:
- Slow Start: The game's initial pacing can be slow, as it takes time to introduce the world, characters, and story. While this deliberate setup enriches the narrative, some players might find the beginning lacking in immediate action.
- Simplicity Hides the Story: The real meat of the game is hidden behind the cozy gameplay, and can feel secondary/be missed for a long time. The game could do a bit of a better job helping move you into the main story.
- Minor Technical Glitches: The game has some minor technical glitches almost apparent of an early access game. That being said the devs are hard at work constantly updating the game and fixing glitches.

Conclusion:
Echoes of the Plum Grove by Unwound Games is a beautifully crafted RPG that shines. Despite a slow start and a bit of a hard to start story line, the game's rich narrative and enchanting world make it a must-play for fans of story-driven cozy adventures. Echoes of the Plum Grove is a "plum" perfect experience, offering a "grove" of rich storytelling and breathtaking visuals that "echo" in your heart long after the final scene.

This is a tremendously enjoyable game! It is obvious right from the beginning how much dedication went into this game, it's full of lovely details both regarding its appearance and its gameplay options. Kudos to the developers for this. 

The graphics are cute, the cut-out optics are a bit awkward when animals turn sideways or you want to place furniture sideways, but that's a tiny setback. I love the details, not only in the locations and people as such but also with the light changing during sundown, the rain or the atmosphere during town festivals. It's just really pleasant to look at and there is so much to discover. Night scenes are a bit difficult though - quite hard on the eyes and therefore not much fun. 

Gameplay is easy. The basics are explained in the beginning and there is also a concise handbook in the game that explains most of the relevant mechanics. There were a few things I had to google but in total you get most of the relevant information and can get right into playing. I found the game a bit too easy for my taste - the survival aspect was not very challenging, at no point did I have any problems with money or food. There is a social aspect of having to build up good relations with the villagers but that was not hard as well - you keep chatting to them a bit and you get showered with gifts in return. And if someone is not that fond of you it doesn't cause any real problems either. 
Overall, I wouldn't mind more challenge. Still, it's a cozy game and it does have several tasks that take some time and effort so it doesn't get boring. 

In addition to farming there are other things to do - mining, chatting with people, trading your stuff, crafting things, fishing, scavenging, getting married. I have now played almost one year in the game (about 31 hours in real time) - the change of the seasons is nicely done and each season brings different challenges, tasks and joys. There are festivals and competitions in town that add something and are nicely executed. 

I am starting to notice that I'm a little less drawn into the game now that most of the small challenges lie behind me - I have heaps of money, a nice house, a nice farm, plenty of friends, a family. The conversations have also started getting repetitive long ago. I don't think that much will follow but so far the game was absolutely worth the buy. 

Controls are mostly nice. I love that I can go places by a click of the mouse, not with the awful WASD-controls that spoil so many games for me. Also there are fast travel signs - you can click on them and get there without having to walk all the way. Lovely idea but there could be more of those signs because getting to some areas is still quite tedious and repetitive. 
Some controls are a bit annoying. - As for options: I love that you can choose some of the options, which in turn makes the game a bit more difficult or easier. I was also pleased to be able to turn off the annoying fishing minigame. It would have been nice to be able to turn off the rather annoying option of men being able to be pregnant as well as some other aspects in that direction but one can fortunately play around that to some extent. Overall the options are nicely done. 

So in total: the game does get a bit repetitive after a while and could use some more challenge, but those are minor setbacks as there is lots to discover and lots to do. For a cozy game it has quite some depth and there are many lovely scenes to discover.

This is an absolutely amazing game so far. I am only in summer of year one, but I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a farming sim this much. Came to town, got set up, suddenly everyone got married within 1 week, left with like 3 single people in the entire village, first one rejects me, contemplated going lesbian, nevermind people died, married a widower, had to befriend my nemesis for that, found a homeless child that lives with me now, have aspirations to get my daughter into the mayors family so I can commit tax evasion. Bridgerton could never. 

The artstyle is also very cute and the entire atmosphere makes it really feel like I am in the 1700s. You rely on the other villagers and their professions to trade a lot of materials, and once a week there is market day with a whole tradeship coming into port. Livestock can (allegedly) be bred and also butchered for meat, which I have not gotten to but am looking forward to. 

There are also a lot of settings to customize your experience, like toggling aging, sickness, food and tool decay or the fishing minigame which is just good QoL. There are of course a few known bugs, but the devs are amazing with their responses and working on fixes already. 

The only negative things I can say about this game is that SO FAR, there is no way to auto-sort your inventory, and some of the item pricing feels a bit unbalanced, as does the cooking when a meal gives you less food or coin than the seperate ingredients would have given. I would also like for new learned recipes to have the name pop up along with a picture of the item, as I have goldfish brain and could not match some of them to anything on my crafting list. But if that is the extent of my complaints, I think it is safe to recommend this game wholeheartedly.

I've enjoyed this game greatly, I dove into it while I had COVID and it was a good distraction. I've tired of most farming sims due to the repetitive nature of them and how they all feel like Stardewvalley wanna-be's. Many aspects of this game set it apart from the crowd. Not to say its with out its flaws, but we'll get to that. The game isn't spared from repetitive parts, but no game is. 

What sets it apart: 

Disease:
I enjoy the emanate threat of the entire village being wiped out by one tourist ship. Maybe I'm a masochist, but it certainty adds a level of realism and spice to the game that other farm sims are lacking. I especially appreciate that there are ways to deal with the sickness (to a degree) so that its never a death sentence, just a challenge. (Unless you're in year one and haven't raised enough money to get inoculated for small pocks and a spotty little miscreant waddles off of the ship and infects your town, but hey soo la voo or what ever the French say.)

Courting:
I like that finding a spouse isn't just "throw gifts at them and have babies". Once you establish that you're courting someone, they ask you to reach X friendship level with the villager they're closest with (usually a family member) and I feel like that's pretty realistic.

Bartering: 
I really really like the fact that you can trade goods for goods. Given the time period its incredibly appropriate. I know a lot of people complain that shops don't have a reliable set of goods every singe day, but I feel that too is realistic. In the real life 1700's supply would depend directly on available trade, seasonality, and availability. It also makes you have to plan in advance, and I enjoy that too. 

Fishing: 
I really appreciate the fact that you can turn the fishing mini game off. A lot. 

Mining: 
Mining in this game isn't how it is in a lot of others in the genera. There is no combat, (at all in this game, the closest you get is combating germs. Lol.) no spending all day in the mines. Just a couple of veins that you can mine daily that supply you with enough to get by, and nothing more. 

Farming:
Though it is annoying to a degree, I appreciate that there isn't any automation for watering your crops. The 1700's (to my knowledge, I'm no scholar) didn't have sprinklers. Irrigation trenches, maybe, but the realistic nature of having to walk around with a watering can and watering each crop is nice. Arduous. But realistic. I also like the fact that you aren't running a farming operation. You aren't planting your entire plot of land and trying to run off a super market chain or what have you. You're just a simple person trying to provide for their family and make a little cash. 

Compost: 
I know a lot of people have complained about the fact that your food rots, but I enjoy realism (pretty obviously at this point in the review) and while I did appreciate being able to store and stash everything for ever to my hearts content in Stardew, having to deal with and plan for rot in this game has been fine to me. It adds a layer of urgency to tasks, and is fixable later in the game. Additionally the fact that you can turn it into compost and fertilize your crops with it is ace in my book. I would like if later in the game something was implemented to where you could add manure from your animals, but I also understand how that would absolutely not be attractive to a lot of other people. 

The Plumb Grove: 
With out spoiling too much for those that haven't played the game, I like the magic/ghost part of the game a lot. It gives you a set goal to work towards as quickly or slowly as you desire. And the witches and their sheep/goats are just fun. 

Children: 
I appreciate that your children grow. Legacy is an entire aspect on its own of the game, but other games where you have kids and they just stay the same for ever the end has always bothered me. I like that their personalities depend on your nurturing and interaction. It makes me a little sad for all of the grumpy villagers. But I like it. 

Things that I feel could be improved: 

Quests: 
I would absolutely love it if I could submit quests to the board and have people bring me stuff I'm looking for how you do for everyone else in the town. Additionally, I feel like you should be able to mail just about anything to other villagers. If you can get gifts in the mail and items from the blacksmith after they're repaired, I feel like there should be some kind of post system or maybe somewhere in the court house you can drop off quest items and then your reward could be sent to you the next day or picked up at where ever the depot is.

Item Descriptions: 
One challenge in the game that I don't appreciate, is trying to figure out how all of the different items work. I'm not sure if I'm just not observant enough, or have over looked it, but a guide or short description in the crafting menu would be helpful.

Housemates: 
I'm sure (or at least I greatly hope) that there is a plan in the future for the NPC's in your house to do more than just stand on the stairs in the way. Same for pets. There are items to place in your house that I feel should be interactive for them, toys for kids, pet beds for pets, bookshelves, etc. And I'm sure its just a matter of time for them to program it, but I look forwards to the change.

Legacy System: 
Getting married and having kids is such an integral and important part of the game, that I hope there is a plan to be able to hand the farm over to your kids prior to your death. Having to wait for your character to die to make sure that the heir marries and has kids feels like a huge waste of very valuable time.  

Heir Relationships: 
Given that your children live in the town for their whole life before you use them as your playable character, I would hope for established relationships in the future. Having no friends or enemies until you take over is a little bland, and just unrealistic. 

I have a lot more I could say about both categories, but this review is already way too long. Over all (tldr) its a very enjoyable game with realistic elements, but its very clear that its an indie game, and as a result there's a few things that could use some work. I have faith that improvements will come in the future, its just a mater of being patient with the devs.

I absolutely adore Echoes of the Plum Grove, it’s one of the most surprisingly addictive cozy games I’ve ever played. The charming visuals and relaxing pace drew me in, but the branching storylines and unexpected risks like disease, aging, and even death kept me hooked. I never imagined a cozy game could have this much depth without sacrificing its warm atmosphere. It’s refreshing to play something that rewards both planning and exploration while still letting you unwind. I just wish more cozy games took these kinds of narrative risks—it makes the entire experience unforgettable.


Why you should play Echoes of the Plum Grove:
	•	Cozy art style with a surprisingly dark and meaningful narrative beneath the surface
	•	Deep generational gameplay: your choices affect future heirs
	•	Characters have personality, relationships, and secrets to uncover
	•	The risk of illness, starvation, or death gives weight to everyday choices
	•	No constant fetch quests
	•	Relaxing pacing with satisfying farming, crafting, and exploring
	•	Incredibly addictive, hours will fly by before you realize it!

I like this game. I have been following it's release. The art style really captivated me, as I love it's flat, cartoony look similar to a paper mario game. The idea to mesh together farming sim mechanics with the longevity of play of a life sim game is truly a combination I have been looking for. I love falling back into an easy routine, as  the small map and frequent teleportation points make traversing the island a real breeze. The game is packed with different mechanics that can diversify a playthrough. If you don't like farming, you can also: raise animals, fish, forage, mine, perform quests, cook, [spoiler] make potions [/spoiler], craft resources and furniture. The trading system is also a very unique change to the farming genre. Instead of a convenient shipping box, you have to go out to town and trade with the folks to get money, seeds, or any other resource which forces you to socialize and potentially find your favorite villager (and potential partner). Villagers have different professions which changes what items they trade, which further incentivises the player to talk with everyone. Another thing I like is the life sim mechanic of having a family legacy to play as when your character dies, as it promotes diversifyng your playthrough and money-making schemes without needing to start anew. One last thing that I love about this game is the LGBTQ+ friendly design. You can choose your pronouns (with a non-binary option) despite your looks, you can marry whatever gender you want, and when you are having a baby with your spouse, the game asks you whether you want to adopt or have a pregnancy, and then you can decide who in the couple gets pregnant (which is very inclusive if you decide that your character is trans... or if you want mpreg to be real, I don't judge). Overall, I recommend this game as a *insert cozy farming sim game* meets the sims type of game.

I think the closest game you can liken Plum Grove to is Kynseed. And I think both of them do different jobs really well. In its current state, for example, family life and forming a lineage is definitely something Kynseed does really well while Plum Grove lacks it in it.

Yet I feel I play more for the town and the villagers than I do for my own lineage. That's a bonus of course because oh no my son married his cousin! That's great drama right there.

Yet I was describing this to my friend and the part I think Kynseed doesn't do well with is how each character looks physically unique so you expect diverse and in depth dialogue. Your expectations are HIGH because the character design is so well done.

Yet the simplicity of Plum Grove gives an unexpected depth because while both utilize the same sort of techniques in the conversations the player has with the people, you form a different attachment to them. To begin with, you always start with the same cast of characters every time you make a new game. While the characters who are children at the time will always be a little unique, they have the same name, same skin color, same hair color, and are from the same families. Yet the fact that those starting villagers and anyone who comes off the boat, is born later, or even yourself looks roughly the same is where you get a blurred line between design uniqueness and personal personification.

To elaborate a bit the Mayor's wife Mary isn't well liked by many fans. She's cold, callous, and rude. Yet she has some interesting dialogue choices due to her personality that gives her a surprising amount of depth. Her personality makes her likely to question the fact that the mayor lives in a large lavish estate, which you could personally headcanon that Mary was a poorer family and she judges the lifestyle she now lives in quite harshly. Maybe she feels her husband shouldn't have the wealth they have when people are scraping by paying ever increasing taxes each week.  Yet someone else could easily consider Mary cold hearted, bitter, and in a loveless marriage where she wants to tear her husband from his seat of power and take it on for herself.

Likewise people like Bridget who is the baker is also cold, sarcastic, a bit mean. She looks unamused and while not cruel her conversations come off as short almost demeaning. Her bread is very popular and she seems to know it. When she tells you "Good luck being a parent" it seems snide compared to maybe the caring way your child says the same line. At least to me. And that's the thing. Everyone reads into the characters something unique and different. Making each villager personal despite the lack of detail. They really are just paperdolls you might have played with as a child. You are coming up with the depth yourself.

I know people will criticize, and already have, for the lack of depth the characters have. But I think that's where a creativity and understanding that you make the characters into what YOU want them to be. You are given the tools: the jobs, the facial expression, the general personalities and hobbies, but through the story telling given by the characters themselves, the world they are in, and the way people gossip about them, characters who seemed flat before are very robust in a very magical way.

I will say its not a perfect game. There are features it lacks that the devs have said is something they will work on. Some people will not like that anyone, regardless of gender, can get pregnant and that might take away from the immersion (I am not one of those people personally). Yet I think the strong points it does have, in the creative aspects of your own personal story telling makes this WAY more like Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, or Caves of Qud than it does Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon. Its a cozy roguelike essentially. A game you will die often in at the beginning if your settings are difficult, many of which can be changed to make it as easy as you wish, but you will always learn from the experience. Figure out things you should and shouldn't do. Like don't eat every mushroom you find and that not every cake is appetizing. Its a game of personal creation and personal exploration than it is a simple farming sim. And I think that makes it one of the best games I've ever played.

Easily one of the most fun farming/cozy games I've played in YEARS. I am an avid Stardew/SoS/Harvest Moon player, and this game is really like if Stardew & Animal Crossings's cousin had a baby with Oregon Trail. It's been so hard to close it and step away, I just want to keep playing and progressing. I would really recommend adjusting the settings AFTER you've played with them normal first, to get a feel for how the game was made to run. I am not ashamed to say I turned off the fishing game - I found it pretty tedious and annoying, and fish is one of the easiest ways to make quick money in this game. I love the flexibility provided as far as controls and even customization for your character once you're IN the game (although I do wish there was a bit more pre-game customization for your character), and honestly one of the only things I'm missing is the ability to name my animals. Some of the point-and-click style controls can feel a bit clunky at first, but once you get used to it it's not bad at all. Best bits of advice I can give - GET INOCULATED and don't interact with strangers from out of town until you do! (Or have your legacy ready to go) Also, wood is a GREAT way to make money early game, but it will mean having to patiently wait and gather two bits of wood per tree (kinda like Animal Crossing) every in-game day to build up the wood for farm buildings - I instead opted to save my wood and fish like a madman in every spare moment of my day, and I sold EVERYTHING the first year that I didn't need to eat to survive and had a chicken coop & barn before fall of my first year. Definitely, there's a lot of flexibility to how you'd like to run your homestead as well. I cannot wait to move on to my next generation and have them raise a family as well. Cannot stress enough - one of the best Cozy games I've played in a very long time. Props to the two person Dev team, you guys are amazing!!! I can't wait for future updates! :3

TLDR: Amazing game, lots of flexibility in how you'd like to approach it & play, totally worth the money if you love Stardew Valley, Harvest Moon, and/or Animal Crossing style games and would like a sort of Oregon Trail danger to it.

Echoes of the Plum Grove is a cool life simulation featuring a novel generational system extending beyond typical farm gameplay. Aside from constructing a farm, one also prepares the farm for winter and makes lasting decisions that shape their family's future.

Strengths:
✔ Adorable papercraft visuals with sweet touches
✔ Intricate generational system: individuals age and die, leaving an inheritance
✔ The combination of farming, town life, and survival keeps things interesting
✔ Dynamic seasons with actual repercussions

Cons:
✖ The start can be trying for newcomers to the series
✖ Less romance interactions than other farming sims
✖ Occasionally sluggish pacing

For life sim fans seeking long-term inspiration and a dose of survival, Echoes of the Plum Grove is a good recommendation!

Obligatory thumbs up, because it was engaging enough to keep me wanting to play until what could be considered the end (basically this game's equivalent of completing the Stardew Valley community center). However, this game is considerably more difficult than a lot of the other farming sims out there, so it felt more like "dang it I'm going to beat this thing!" as opposed to "I just can't put it down!" So if you like farming games and want something more challenging than usual that also has a unique plot, this game is probably for you. To be fair, also, some of the features that make it more difficult can be turned off, but I stubbornly let my gamer pride keep me from doing that.

Also I feel the need to mention that this game's crafting system is one of its drawbacks. For example, crafting a smelter required the use of items that are crafted ON said smelter, leaving you to have to buy them anyway, which, early on, is pretty difficult. It felt like a bit of a slog to get things started and build things up, which is why I don't see myself doing multiple playthroughs.

So in short, has its flaws, still engaging, the challenging aspects will appeal to some but it won't be for everyone.

Sure, I know that's Life, but I play games to get away from Life. 

On the plus side, I was pleased to see that this colonial village was pretty open-minded for the time period and had no problem with me courting another man. In fact, the first marriage announcement I received was for a same-sex couple. I thought, "Oh, my God! (Yay, verily?) There's another gay couple in town! I should go meet them with a casserole."

It turned out, we weren't all that rare. Pretty much EVERY marriage announcement after that was for same-sex couples. I'd stumbled into the colonial equivalent of Fire Island. (Old man reference. Look it up, whippersnappers.) The next issue was, how are all these gay male and female couples supposed to have children without committing adultery? The game doesn't have poly relationships (sadly), nor does it have an orphanage. I gather if you have diseases turned on, you can wipe out half the adult population with smallpox and give yourself a pool of orphans to choose from. I... did not choose this option. 

Fear not! Our little LGBTQ+ colony also had mpreg! I got knocked up twice and wandered around town holding my belly, passing several other men who were likewise with child. In fact, even among the few straight couples in town, it wasn't unheard of for the man to be the one who got pregnant. Ah, the wonders of 17th Century medicine!

I swear, I did not select the "Children of Dorothy" checkbox under options. Fortunately, the game does have other options a player might find useful, from whether or not food rots to whether or not people get sick. You can even turn off aging, though I'm not sure if that prevents others in the village from aging. 

At any rate, I'm enjoying it and still haven't given up after 47 hours. My biggest issue (apart from the "everyone is dying" thing) is how fast things rot in my inventory. I wanted to have it on, since it would be ridiculous to have fruit remain fresh for months, but on average everything rots after just a few days. This makes it impossible to keep basic supplies on hand, so when someone asks you to bake them a pumpkin pie, you'll have everything you need except sugar, and all your pumpkins are guaranteed to turn to mush before you can find someone who has sugar in stock. I love the dark humour of the developers when they conceptualised this farming game set in the 1700s. The characters are simply adorable visually but what is remarkable is the different conversations that you can have with the NPCs. I didn't expect my pregnant spouse to complain about his favourite food or my children to bemoan the constant presence of me because they have plenty of chores (those brats). 
You need to talk to the NPCs and they give you delightful nuggets that would help you. eg. Watering twice a day in spring will make your plants grow faster.

The main quest is rather straightforward: survive...survive and survive. No, I'm kidding. (I think) You have to complete several quests to help the spirits stuck in the limbo. After that, it's really up to you. There isn't side quests to keep you going back to the game.
Visually, it is really a pretty game, matched with a delightful soundtrack. I really enjoyed autumn. The warm, golden hues along with its sombre music create a very pleasant experience.

OK, Let's talk about some mechanics.
The game is tough and the developers know it. You have options of turning off hunger and illness which is very useful at the start. If I want to be truly nit picky, there is no constant market to buy things that you pick, which makes it difficult to start a sustainable income. You actually need to know who has the deepest pockets (ahem, the mayor) Don't worry, the locals will eventually have more gold to buy your products if you sell things to them constantly.
Hunger is a major issue at the start since it is expensive to buy food. The easiest recipe, bread, requires egg and flour. That means you need to have the resources to build a coop to have chicken and you'll also need to grow wheat to have flour : not too doable until at least 2 weeks into the game.
Next, the fruit trees.
I think they must be considered a luxury item for year 2 and later since it takes 15 days for them to grow and bear fruits. Given that the season is only 21 days long, by the time the fruit trees are grown, you'll be in a new season. That means if you missed planting these trees by the first week, don't expect to have any fruits.
Next, events.
I love the unique conversations of NPCs during the lead up to the event. However, I think Autumn as a season is poorly designed for events, which is a waste. There are two major events which is Halloween and Harvest festival in a 21-day season. There was little hints about preparing for Halloween and I was caught by surprise. I was quite frustrated that I could only give the kids stones for trick and treat because I didn't know that you need to prepare caramel apples (1 caramel + 1 apple) As mentioned earlier, the fruit trees take 15 days to mature. That means that you can't have apples even if you planted them at the start of the season since Halloween is on day 12. Besides, caramel can only be bought from ships that visit during the weekend and you can buy only 1 each time. See the problem? You probably need to prepare from spring just to have enough apples for 7 kids. Anyway, it feels a little like the events is set up to fail even though it can be so cute to see the kids running around in their costumes. Now, you have to prepare for the harvest event in a week while prepping for winter..... YIKES.
Finally, FOOOD.
I used a guide for this after I realised the complexity of having sustainable food. Most of the recipes require produce from multiple seasons which mean that you need to stockpile while turning off the item decay option. I think I settled for buttered cod for the all cod seasons. I think that there should be more recipes that uses only produce within the same season so that cooking can be explored.

In all, it is a game worth playing for hours. There are some rough edges that can be smoothed and the developers have made it easier for us to survive by allowing us to turn off troublesome options like hunger, illness and decay.

The game never communicates this limitation, which makes the experience feel unfair.

The daily gameplay loop also becomes repetitive quickly. You end up doing the same tasks every day with very little variation. Resource gathering, especially, feels tedious. Wood is surprisingly hard to come by unless you constantly shake trees or buy from NPCs, and iron is even worse. There’s so little ore available, and the furnace’s 3:1 ratio (three ores for one iron) makes it nearly impossible to be self-sufficient.

On top of that, the game has several technical and quality of life issues. Bugs and controller responsiveness is inconsistent. Storage management is one of the biggest frustrations. Storage isn’t shared with crafting objects, so you constantly have to take items out manually before using anything. Even at the craft table, you might try to make something and the craft panel shows you’re missing materials even though the materials are literally sitting in the storage box right next to it. Interacting with objects is also clunky. For example, clicking the preservation jar should bring up a popup asking what you want to add, instead of forcing you to select the item and pressing space and also needing to locate the item in the inventory to bring it to the firat hotbar is unintuitive.

Instructions are also lacking, especially when it comes to babies and some other mechanics. Some systems just aren’t explained well, leaving players to figure things out through trial and error.

Overall, Echoes of Plum Grove has a great foundation. The generational gameplay and storybook style world are genuinely charming. But the game needs better balance, clearer rules, more polish, and smoother quality of life features to truly reach its potential.

[h3][u]A cute game that will appeal more to certain players than to others[/u][/h3]

I see that, once again, Echoes of Plum Grove has fallen into the dreaded "mostly positive" category. I'm writing this review in hopes of fixing that! 
For those who played Paper Mario 64, this game will likely feel as nostalgic to you as it was to me. The art is simple but charming, the music fits perfectly, and the cozy farming mechanics align a lot with games like Harvest Moon or Stardew Valley.  

[h3]🍇Unique lite survival🍇(toggleable)[/h3]
This game has "survival" in terms of hunger, rot, disease, and fatigue (as well as aging, though I don't consider this as much of a survival mechanism because it's not one that can be directly influenced). ALL of the aforementioned mechanics are toggleable. Meaning, you can have as much (or as little) challenge as you like! 

Personally, I never found any of these mechanics very challenging. Food is handled (for life) of you have a fishing rod. If you can't fish, there's seasonable foragables year-round. Most NPCs sell some sort of food (even just a raw plum or a clam!) and if you've made any friends, you will likely be gifted a present every day in your mailbox (may or may not be food). 
Rot, much like in another game, Vintage Story, proves to be a sought-after ingredient in fertilizers, making food spoilage less of a kick to the gut (and even desirable!). In my 100 in-game days of playing, my character, Eleanor Winters, got sick once (common cold). Though, I did visit the local doctor and pay (iirc) $500 to be "inoculated" by the second half of the first year. 
If you want a survival challenge, this game isn't it. Go play Green Hell instead.


[h3]🍇Rimworld-esque random events and generations🍇[/h3]

What makes Echoes of Plum Grove most enjoyable (beyond the art-style) is the simple character design. The villagers are somewhat generic, but this works in the game's favor! Like Rimworld pawns, falling in love with these little Plum Grove folks is easy because they're more of a blank slate for the story to be delivered on. 

For example, I fell in love with the carpenter, Jack Watt. But he got married on Spring 4th! While you can (optionally) murder your enemies, this wasn't a route I was invested in, myself. So, I settled to marry his brother, William. By the end of Spring, I'd managed to net myself a marriage bouquet and a copper wedding ring, but would he say yes? Would he marry someone else before I could propose? I was inoculated, but was he? 
I found myself absolutely on the edge of my seat to see if my plan to marry William would be a success. Now, coming onto the end of my second Spring, my original character, Eleanor, has grown old! William and I had three kids, Iris, Darrell, and Bruce. Darrell married two days into adulthood and Bruce is still but a child. 
When I (Eleanor) finally pass away, who will I play as? Do I get a choice? Will I know when I die and have the chance to say my farewells? The characters lack depth, but I find myself invested in them anyways. Making my own stories and predictions for what will go wrong (or right!) in our little colony of Honeywood. 


[h3]🍇A cozy game at heart🍇[/h3]

Now that you know there are optional survival elements, let's talk about what Plum Grove is and is not. In the past, I've struggled to hold interest in games that are [i]too cozy[/i]. 
Games like Stardew Valley and Harvest Moon are well-crafted, but progress too slowly to hold my interest. Rune Factory is more my style with the fantasy story and combat. 
Plum Grove, in my opinion, is a happy medium. While there is no combat, the risk of disease and death manages to spice the game up just enough. Lobster fishing got me an upgraded house with income left to spare and is just challenging enough to make me keep going. I also make it a point to befriend everyone in town before I die (or before they do!), giving me more goals beyond customizing my farm. 

But for folks who adore the idyllic life of Stardew or Harvest Moon, Plum Grove should be a delight! Your massive farm allows for detailed customization, as well as a broad range of craftables, dyable clothing, and interior design choices. There's also a growing variety of animals to buy and care for!

[h1] Love farming sims and The Sims? You'll love this~ [/h1]

Started this…3 days ago? And have already played 32 hours, including playing for basically 2 days straight, staying up until midnight, to keep going. You can call me officially addicted. (And I haven’t even finished the main plot yet, or fully upgraded my farm!)

Most farming sims lose a lot of playability once you get married and/or have kids, and I have trouble sticking with those games past that point. But Plum Grove ENCOURAGES (if not soft-requires) you to get married and have kids in the early-game, so you have the rest of the game to enjoy your social accomplishments!

Some more specifics (and will update if there’s more significant details to add):

[h2] The “Glows” [/h2]
- This game promises connections and community, and it delivers! You love the gossip and growth of the characters, and get to know them over time throughout their lives. [spoiler] (And afterlives! I love that you can talk to their ghosts—it’s such a great circle of life (and death)! They recount their previous passions and want to check-in on their lost loves. The ghosts make everything more poignant). [/spoiler]

- While there is still a lot of overlapping dialogue between villages, the dialogue itself is well-written and interesting. As someone who’s played (way too much) of Animal Crossing, Rune Factory, and Harvest Moon games (and many adjacent farming sims…), the dialogue isn’t saccharine or trite, and, back to the good ol’ days of the first Animal Crossing game, certain villagers can even be genuinely cantankerous and mean (which make the personality contrasts all the more fun!).

- If you love the genetics/freewill systems in Sims, you’ll get addicted to this! The children believably take after their parents, and I have a blast looking at their names/appearances and remembering which villager wound up with whom to spawn these new [strike] pawns [/strike] youths.

- Love how everyone has a profession, schedule, hobby, and unique personalities!

- FINALLY! A farming sim whose family members finally DO something!! Not just minor chores, too, like (unnecessarily) watering your pet’s dish (looking at you, Stardew), but actually watering and taking care of all of your crops. 

- The actual PLOT! (No spoilers here, go play it. :P )

- For an Early Access indie game, the controls are smooth even on a Steam Deck, and I haven’t run into any noticeable glitches so far. I also appreciate the Settings that let you make the game as stress-free or challenging as you’d like, without feeling unfair. The game also feels pretty balanced with the recent stone/lumber updates.

- LGBTQIA+ marriages, pregnancies, and representation overall~ (Something modern farming sims are only recently catching onto!)

- The town actually feels "alive." Again, I've played my fair share of farming sims, and one of the biggest gripe (next to not having rival marriages/kids (ANOTHER THING THIS GAME DELIVERS!!)) are huge maps that feel like ghost towns, with the characters feeling like they're on a predictable treadmill every single day. But the hobbies/personalities/professions all do a great job interplaying to make each character feel like a true individual. Each person's schedule is a little bit unpredictable and yet still habitual enough that you get a "feel" for each villager as you would real people, and the town feels more lived in and active as a result. Each area of the map feels necessary with [i] something [/i] going on at all times.

[h2] The “Grows” [/h2]

[h3] Depth [/h3]
- Another review mentioned how this game has a lot of promising mythological aspects, including mermaids, pirates, and witches. However, these elements don’t “talk” too much with each other. I would love for the lore/story to go deeper so there’s more to learn and do with each of these groups. Right now, the witches are the only really fleshed out plot, but I could see future DLCs exploring the mermaid and pirate plotlines. 

- Family having more actions/animations in the house. For whatever reason, they seem to just cluster on the entranceway in the first house or the stairway for the 2nd-upgraded house. Your character can pass through them so they’re not in the way, so it would be cute if they had idle actions, like stirring the pot or sitting/laying on furniture, or playing with the toys you can buy.

[h3] Quality of Life [/h3]

- Ability to filter/organize items in your inventory/storage.

- Make it easier to choose your family’s jobs, and to see their skills (you can only see your character’s).

- I know this would require a lot of additional artwork, but a nice stretch goal would be able to rotate your furniture, so you can have even more customization.

[h2] Verdict [/h2]

Overall, if you're concerned about Early Access games, I'd recommend Echoes of the Plum Grove with confidence. It plays smoothly and has enough content to feel like a complete game, with any additional content in the future just adding to its replayability/longevity. The areas for growth are only minor, and the genuine community connections, generations, and town that actually feels "lived in" make this game an easy farming sim favorite.

This has quickly become one of my favorite farming games. I love how unique it is, from being set in the 1700's, so the emphasis on generational gameplay, to the amount of chaos you have to deal with on a regular basis. There are a lot of challenges built into the game, but the settings allow a lot of flexibility to turn off harder settings. I've been playing with everything on except the fishing mini-games, since I don't like mini-games in general and the one in this game is rather terrible. 

THINGS I LIKE:
- The challenge. It's a difficult game with all the settings turned on. If you're not going to adjust the settings, you have to be willing to put up with some frustration and grinding, particularly early on. But this also makes it more rewarding when you get to a place when you're comfortable in the game and don't need to grind as much. 
- The  seasons. Seasons are only 21 days, which means you move through your character's life at a fairly reasonable pace so you can get to the next generation by the time you're bored with the current one. Also means that winter, which is generally the most boring season in farm sims, is less of a drag. I also love how much the weather varies. Winter isn't just all the same amount of snow; it fluctuates day to day. Days are shorter in winter, longer in summer, just like IRL. 
- The art style and world. Everything is very pretty. The map is relatively large. It does get less exciting the more you wander around looking for the same resources day after day, but it's still very nice looking. I love the character art. It was a little hard to adjust to the 2.5D because I've never played a game like that, but once I was used to it I really like it. 
- For being set in 1700, the game is fairly inclusive. Anyone can marry anyone, and anyone can get pregnant. There's also adoption options. 
- The festivals and events are all very cute. There's lot necessarily a ton to do at every since one, BUT I love that people actually move around and do stuff. In a lot of games, the characters just stand there doing nothing as you move around, but in EotPG, they participate in the activities and chat with each other. 
- When you move onto the next generation, their skills reset but you still maintain your inventory and all the recipes and stuff you've learned. I like that you have something you can still focus on for your next generation by building their skills back up, without making you feel like you've lost ALL your progress. 
- There is no shipping bin/box. At first this annoyed me, but I actually ended up liking that you have to go interact with the town to sell stuff. It adds to the challenge. And almost every villager is capable of buying from you (although their money amounts vary each day).
- While the game lacks conveniences like a shipping bin, it has a few other nice quality of life details. The inventory you get is large right from the beginning, and you have immediate access to fast-travel around town. 
- The magical elements. It's not enough to overshadow everything else, it's just a fun touch. 
- It's fun to get to know the villagers. They're simple but quirky. Are they super deep? No. But do I care? Also no. In a game where people drop like flies, I don't really need to be emotionally devastated every time someone is unalived. But it's fun to see how they pair up over the generations, who kicks the bucket early, and who takes over what profession. I've also had my current character go on a bit of a murder spree to cull some of the villagers and encourage new blood to come in. Sorry not sorry. 

THINGS I DISLIKE:
- Resources like trees and rocks do not regenerate on your farm. While it's nice in a lot of ways to not have to stay on top of keeping your farm clean, there aren't enough other ways to gather wood and stone. You can shake trees in town for wood but it's very grindy, and you can only get a few rocks per day in the mines. Occasionally you can lucky out and get these resources from villagers, but it's rare. 
- The mining is tedious. It takes more time to walk down the shaft to the mining spots than it does to actually mine. Once there, there are only two spots to mine from (and later a third) and you don't get very much from them each day. I get that it's probably meant to be more realistic to have to walk down deeper, but I could live without actually having to witness it. Same with the journey down to Limbo. It's unnecessarily long. You can use various things to make your character walk faster, but these are still a chore.
- Not a lot of options for decorations, for both indoor and outdoor. But the game is young, so it's entirely possible this stuff will be added to later.
- There's a lot of little tutorials, but there are still quite a few things that aren't explained very well. I've had to look up what a lot of the artisan machines need for you to put in them, since they don't tell you in game. I also had to look up how long each life stages last. There's a progress bar for the pages on adults, but that's the only stage you get it for. And it still doesn't tell you how long the progress bar goes for. 
- There are a few other things I dislike, but I think I'm going to raise them as suggestions before I complain about them in a review.

It is absolutely not a perfect game, there are small but infrequent bugs and the social/family aspects of the game are pretty bare bones, but it is a good game that I enjoy nonetheless, and keep in mind that this was made by only two developers. 

The artstyle is adorable and pleasing to look at. The music can be repetitive but it's relaxing to zone out to.

 The gameplay is good, there is a story but it's definitely not the most in depth and there is little to no reward for following/completing it. Where it really shines is the various randomized quests you can take on from the villagers. They always give you something to do, and you never know what kind of cool things you could get as a reward. Just be careful during selection because some quests are impossible to complete if they ask for something out of season, and you can't discard quests until they naturally expire on their own.

The aging system is fun, seeing the original NPCs experience different lives each playthrough is a cool touch, and it's fun to see how different your town looks year by year. Getting to play as your kids is pretty awesome too, but I do wish you could have the option to play as a child if your heir is still young when your main character dies. It feels weird to just suddenly age up to an adult when the kids born before you are still kids! Perhaps it could be an optional choice, for those who just want to move on and get their character married, but I would love to experience my character's childhood to feel immersed. Gameplay wouldn't have to change at all either, because you simply inherited the farm as your new job!

The difficulty is very customizable, you can remove aging, illness, minigames, and item decay to make your experience as stressful or peaceful as you want. All I really do is remove the fishing minigame because it's a lot of work for not a lot of reward. I also only take on one quest at a time because I get overwhelmed easily, but I've seen plenty of people with huge lists of quests to occupy themselves with if that's more your style!

Overall, there is room to improve, but the devs slowly continue to add updates and content as well as bug fixes, and I'm excited to see where things go from here! I would definitely recommend this to anyone who likes farming/life sims, and the actual Sims franchise as well!

(and here's a free reminder that the tougher features, like disease, death, decay, etc., are all completely optional and can be turned off any time - you can fully customize how hard you want the game to actually be!)

things i like the most from the game:
[list]
[*]the art style! reminiscent of the paper mario series which i LOVE so there is probably some bias there. the hair and clothing options are very cute.
[*]the soundtrack is beautifulllll overall (except two particular tracks that gave me uneasy feelings, but i would adjust the music volume for them).
[*]the emote wheel which definitely added to the immersion: dancing with the other villagers at the winter gala, bopping for apples on halloween, expressing sadness and crying during funerals, sitting and enjoying nature in the forest while my child is foraging nearby, etc.
[*]the freedom to pretty much play how you want - having the ability to adjust certain gameplay settings is something i was super thankful for. i didn’t like having to stress over hunger and sleep so i toggled those off very early + adjusted to slow aging to really make my first playthrough enjoyable at the pacing i would prefer, no added pressure.
[*]the options allowed when it comes to children - pregnancy or adoption, and choosing who will be pregnant if it’s the former.
[*]the option to choose your clothing preference for weddings.
[*]the variety of traits and observing the different kinds of people that villagers turn out to be (…however i’m admittedly the kind of player to save before midnight and reload a day multiple times to make sure a villager gets positive traits + looks decent. i’ve death caked several cruel type villagers and wonder who that actually makes the cruel one… couldn’t be me right? ….nah) it’s interesting to see how different your game can play out from another player’s when we all start with the original lineup of villagers.
[/list]

things i didn’t like from the game:
[list]
[*]probably the biggest one: lack of a sorting feature for your storage/inventory. i think i read somewhere that they were looking into this, and hopefully it comes in a future update. for now though it makes organizing your stuff a daunting task.
[*]house decoration has several limitations. you can’t place things on top of rugs. and there is a particular bug where when you line up objects a certain way that creates some sort of invisible wall and it drives me INSANE. there are also some craftable items (like for crafting artisan items) that i wish we were given the option to place outside. it also would be nice to have some sort of option for the exterior of the house upgrades, but that’s not really a big deal.
[*]besides the bug mentioned above, the other bugs. there is one i think they’re working on fixing where your family just stands at the stairs - i’ve gotten used to it by now after playing for several in-game years but it is mildly annoying. there is another bug i’ve encountered at least once where the time randomly froze and i was unable to interact with things or save. this caused me to force restart and lose my day of progress which was quite frustrating, but at least it was only that day. another bug is the inaccurate baby happiness/hunger meter when you’re outside of your house. the bottle indicator to feed the baby also doesn’t show up for me sometimes - not sure why - but i resolve this by picking up the crib with the hammer and placing it down again, which resets their meter.
[*]the events do not come with clear instructions in game. [spoiler] it was a sad experience to show up to the harvest festival for the first time without having items prepared for the grange display because it didnt mention it beforehand in the invitation. [*]regarding the storyline, i do wish it delved a little deeper. [spoiler] learning more about limbo, timothy and your relationship with him, astra and her history, etc. would be pretty nice. it would be nice to know just a little bit more background about the original cast of villagers (besides the whitfields) but i understand that they're only there at the start. [/spoiler]
[/list]

overall, it’s a unique life sim that has a lot to offer and i would definitely recommend this game to friends. in spite of the cons listed, i’ve had a really fun experience playing so far, and right now i’m facing a dilemma of whether i want to continue my legacy after grinding all achievements or starting a fresh second playthrough. it’s also cool to see the active discord community and posts from the devs with what they’re working on. looking forward to future updates that may be added over time  ^^
