Original Post:
Love the generational theme.  I have played a 183 hours in the last few weeks which speaks to its play ability.  Just started my second save.  

Hint to new players: Read topics available in the Tutorial Tab of the Inventory Menu.  This helped me a lot as this game is a new take on farming simulation.  It plays a bit differently than other farming games but that is not a drawback.  

Also: There is not many spoilers available at this time online so it is a great pick for someone who dislikes spoilers.

Preface: I love this game for what it is. More people need to go into the game knowing what to expect so as not to be disappointed because they wanted a completely different game.

This is a simple farming game in the style of Paper Mario, limited dialogue/relationship building, limited decorating, but lots of farming and quests to fulfill. Don't go in thinking this is a deeply involved relationship simulator with multiple story archs wildly different endings with whirlwind mysteries kind of game.

This game works best for people with a good imagination for headcanons & creating their own narratives for everyone because you won't get a solid backstory from any villagers, (aside from one very obvious one). I liken this to playing Sims for multiple generations, you invent personalities and backstories. 

The game is very simple in terms of story and dialogue. I can respect that because it also has a lot of gameplay accessibility options to make the game less of a grind which I like.  And there's controller support that's awesome.

The game advertises itself as "Cozy with Consequences" but I think they just mean "consequences for everyone who gets on your bad side." You can poison the whole town, no one grows suspicious, your relationship meters with everyone are unaffected, and everyone keeps accepting your Death Cake as gifts. The "consequences" are taxes, diseases, raising animals for food, and death. 

There are no negative social repercussions for decisions you make. You won't get price gouged for being rude to the shop keeper or get discounts for being sweet to the Mayor. There are weddings, funerals, festivals, farmers markets, and competitions. Zero consequences for not going to any of them. Your consequences are now you have no friends to give you gifts.

You only benefit from going to festivals and funerals is everyone gathering in one place so you're able to mass gift or talk to everyone at once. The more friends you have the more gifts you can get sent to your mailbox.

There is no deep mystery/lore to uncover about different towns people, there is *one* tidbit of lore about one very obvious person in town. Overall, you can expect all the townspeople are copy pastes of personality types and dialogue.

Villagers will say "Boy do I have some gossip for you!" then talk about how much they like the smell of bread from the bakery. Its got so much dialogue potential but it tends to fall a little flat. 

Imagine Animal Crossing level of limited dialogue based on personality and hobbies. There is no villager lore or backstory for 99% of the villagers. You invent and imagine whatever you like. You will see and hear the same dialogue from different villagers repeatedly.

Yes you can get married and have kids but there is zero relationship specific backstory dialogue. Other than your partner calling you darling and saying "I love you" at the end of a conversation.  

Your kids will call you mom/dad. Your family members can give you gifts every few days, sometimes its money, other times its sticks and dirt. You can send your kids to school to increase their skills but I've yet to see how that benefits you. You can send your kids to do apprenticeships and earn money, fun having one kid being a Blacksmith and the other a baker, you always have access to their shops by talking to your kids.

Marry any of the shop keepers/crafters you will not get a discount on any items, you will get to "collect" their wages every day which can be anywhere from 10 to 200 coins which may help. 

There is no family tree to look at and keep track of beyond the initial family.

Looking at villagers and their families they're all ordered randomly, it would make more sense for families to be grouped.



Gameplay:
The accessibility options is fine for gameplay. But I'd like to see some colorblind accessibility options. Just make things more distinct in for different colorblind types.

I love the gameplay accessibility. If you go to your settings and turn on and off settings that will make the game tedious or grindy such as taxes, hunger, energy, tool breaking, etc. No one judges you for settings that make the game more fun for you. I promise. 

I will say its a challenging game in terms of money. Earning money is ROUGH if you're unfamiliar what to focus your time on. I spent too much time floundering between trying to complete quests, buying items for crafting, and trying to pay the taxes every week and barely scraped by. Turn off Taxes in the Options Menu for the less stressful playing experience.


Decorating/Customizing:
You can decorate your cabin if you *really* want but honestly early game its a waste of money since there's limited room and so much you need to craft to even make a penny, invest in a flour mill, preserve bucket, drying rack, and candy maker (for autumn halloween)

Decorating is really lacking. 
For Wallpaper/Carpet: You can use the item ONCE and then its destroyed if you replace it. Place a red wallpaper, you get a fancy blue one and put it up to test it out dont like it and look back at your inventory and the red one is gone forever. Bye bye 120 gold. Good luck finding that specific wallpaper again. You should be able to preview wallpaper or be warned by using one you replace the other one forever.

You can buy a massive carpet, but not be able to place any furniture on it or very near it. Takes up too much space with zero benefit. A lot of the Craftable food prep items are *not* placable outside so you're stuck with having them inside your cabin if you want to make money.

Maybe this'll change in the future?

Making Money Tips:
For making money I suggest buying a fishing rod, lure, and lantern with lantern oil. Turn off taxes, energy and hunger and fish all through out the night from 9pm to 7am at the pond near your house. Collect fish to fill your inventory and sell them the next morning to which ever shop keeper you can find. Once you unlock the lagoon past the broken bridge fish there from 9pm to 8am. If you can preserve and dry your food items it'll sell for a *little* bit more.

You are limited at collecting wood from shaking all trees and what wood you clear from your farm initially, each piece of wood sells for 10 coins. 

Quality of Life Suggestions: 
-Automatic stacking: Often times placing items in your pocket or storage will just stack things beside one another instead of in the same stack via quality.
-Crafting from Storage: Maybe its an unlockable thing but it would make crafting simpler.
- Gates should open Inward instead of out: When playing the game by mouse clicks (instead of WASD or Arrows) has you spinning or walking in place quite a bit forcing you if you try to go through gates that open outward or at the Witch's Shack in the Bog.
- Craftable lanterns offer a small dot of light with zero glow around the lantern providing almost no benefit to crafting other than taking up a square on your farm maybe its a bug?
-Preview wallpapers on the walls before applying them. Once applied its fine if you lose the wallpaper you covered up. At least give us confirmation "adding this wallpaper permanently replaces the old one are you sure"

About: 
It is a game more based at a time period when you didn't have electricity, sprinklers or the modern conveniences of modern day Farm simulators. Do not compare this to Harvest Moon or Stardew, it is definitely a Unique game in the farming Genre.

How is it Unique?
-First off, families and death. Your character will die either it be natural causes, disease or your own blunder. You can spread disease and kill off half your village (No you do not own a village, ur just a new Farmer). So if you die (I haven't yet) your child is supposed to take over or I assume it's game over?

-It's a slow burn casual game, you can do alot in the first year but it's very slow and has a slow rate of pacing while maintaining other moving parts at a slightly faster speed. Honestly I believe it's more balanced and realistic to a farming simulator. This focuses much more on management on resources including time. 

-You are not constricted to go to bed by 1, you can make your own schedule but your character needs to eat and sleep. 
-You can take quest, fail and not have any consequences. 

-You can insult people or be a nice person and not insult them. Is there a benefit to this? Apparently there is. 

-Yes you do pay taxes, which this brings another topic of difficulty. You can make it as hard or as easy as you want, you can turn off taxes and disease with a few other options. It is a very casual roleplaying game. 

Cons for people who are used to Modern Farming games:

-Slow, no you won't upgrade everything in the year. 

-Story progression: It's there, but i still haven't found the locket.

-No wood/stone grinding, you must do this daily with a max of 40~ wood a day after you clean your farm. Stone is even harder to find. (To remedy this you will have to check shops everyday and buy it as almost twice the markup you'd sell for). Mining is limited to 4 nodes which give some nice things but you'll have to visit every few days. 

-Anything that has to do with automation, electricity, modern QoL or sprinklers forget it. You do however have the ability to have children and make them farm slaves. Along with your spouse. 

Final Thoughts?
-It's not super challenging, tho it's very slow compared to other games of the same genre. Yet, it's very different and unique that it's quite refreshing and fun to play. It is definitely not for everyone and this will take hours to make progression for you do rely on your neighbors and other villagers to make a living. Personally, I've really enjoyed it, had very few annoying moments (only when i can't get to someone's house cause they live inside a closed business or i can't find the person im looking for). I only say, don't go into this thinking it's like stardew, harvest moon or modern genres. It is a game that feels like it's for people who like the less fantasy side of things and more realism but still has the fun parts of a game like this. (there are witches).

What surprised me the most of this game was how attached I managed to get to villagers with a very faint personality. Usually I don't care much about NPC’s, even when well written, but with Echoes it was the opposite. I married the drunkard bad boy of the village, I insult the witch and the teacher's daughter every time I see them just because I don't like their faces. And today the old trapper who lived in the wood died, and I really liked him (such an adorable old man), so I went to his funeral and used the crying animation to convey all of my sadness. Maybe because they don't have a deep personality, I can make my own and be more free to see them as I want. 

They might not tell you lines and lines of texts about their life, but that didn't prevent me from loving or hating them and coming up with my own backstories for them. I was sad when Rowland the blacksmith died, because I traded with him almost daily, and he apprenticed my son. I went to his funeral and sobbed the whole time. In my mind, we were great friends. And my relationship with the Mayor's son was a weird one, as I thought him to be a snob and privileged, but then he became a tailor and we became friends. For me, their "flatness" was less annoying than other games' stereotyped characters that I couldn't get to like. The more “personality” developers put into characters, the more flat they seem to me. I like Echoes and the Sims, because it leaves enough to the imagination that they feel more real to me instead of me relying on the creator to tell me who the people are. The characters may also be a bit flat but the dialogue is witty at times. It’s also a lot of quest fulfilling which I personally enjoy. I’m a big farm sim lover anyways so I’m happy fishing, farming, crafting to fulfil quests.

The threat of illnesses that can potentially kill half of your village (maybe your romantic interest too), the need to produce food to eat unless you want to starve, and some other "less cozy" mechanics were a fresh breath. I like farming sims, but they get boring for me when you start to set up your farm and just get tons of money that you don't even know how to spend. With Echoes, there's always something draining the money you have saved. The game has indeed a slower pace, and the beginning might seem a big grindy, but for me that's a plus, cause it means I will have things to do with my future generation. Being poor is fun, at least for me.

I enjoyed the game because I loved the art style and I just see it as a cozy game where I don’t rush to get iron, nails and stone. I quite liked the fact that I can’t rush things and I’m kinda at the mercy of what the townsfolk have to trade/sell. I go to the shop everyday and when they’re there they’re there and when not I either wait or go search for them. There’s no rush as I don’t have to immediately upgrade my house or build a barn. I don’t need an ice box yet because I get gifted enough food from the villagers and can easily dry food on the drying rack or preserve it, etc. You can make it as peaceful or “harrowing” as you like, can allow aging, diseases, poison etc. or not! You can customise it in the settings to be as challenging or cozy as you want, such as changing the lifespan, durability of tools and items, if you have an energy meter or if you pay taxes etc. The game doesn’t overly hold your hand, there’s things you can only get by trading with the townsfolk or doing quests to start with. 

This game is unlike any other, so don't go in with expectations. Like I mentioned, most farm games have well fleshed characters but in a game where one of the goals is aging and dying, it's not realistic to have fleshed out characters. Especially when characters kind of jump jobs and families (mayors wife became a lesbian butcher after her husbands death) it's immensely hard to make character backstories that would make sense. Especially when you are present for back story and like know their parents and grandparents. The characters are meant to be completely replaceable.

The way I see it is it's similar socially to Cult of the Lamb. NPC’s have some "base personality types" (as*hole, sweet, drunk) and you can have favorites and love some, but at the end of the day, even if you don't sacrifice them, they die of old age. With that in mind, I quite enjoyed the game. It's like Rimworld met Harvest Moon. There is a little excitement with trying to survive but not in the desperate Don't Starve or combat styled games. To me it's quite beautiful to see a game that shows "Rome wasnt built in a day". Like your character won't get a whole farm set up in their lifetime, but it's ok, someone will take over. And though there are some quirks, most of them have to do with the game not quite being complete.

To me, I think it is far more "original" than people credit it for. I guess that's because it contains "farming". I see it more as a survival and legacy builder game if you want to play it that way - and that's also an originality point to me. How many "cozy farming games" allow you to increase or decrease difficulty on the fly? Or give you the option to play several saves at varying difficulties so you can turn everything off and focus on the residents of Honeywood or make a new save with everything ramped up so you are challenged to survive in this 1701 era with all the hardships life can throw at you. 

If I have to find a flaw for the game, it is that it's still a young game, so it has room for improvement. I have no problem waiting for new features and content to be added, so it doesn't frustrate me that much. As for the Devs, you can really tell this was a labour of love for them and they are super active with the community- so I think it would be safe to say there’s more to come with this game. Basically, I love this game. And I highly highly recommend it. There’s a lot of typical farm stuff as well as stuff with ghosts and being able to murder your NPC’s.

Dear friend - this is a tale of my life in Plum Grove. 

One sorrowful day, I was washed up on a strange island. The towns people who rescued me insisted that I must take over the farm of my drowned friend, whose optimism was the source of so much sunshine to those who knew him. 

So trying to carry on my friend's hopeless optimism, I set about trying to make the most of the life that was bequeathed to me, which was hard because I was penniless and utterly friendless - but that doesn't save you from paying your weekly taxes now does it? 

I had to survive on weeds and wild berries while I sold the fruits of my harvests to the locals just to buy some nails and pay my dues. When I had the energy I would spend whatever remained of my day fishing and doing chores for the locals -- when they weren't asking for very complicated recipes or furniture which were beyond my simple means.  

As the year passed, I made no friends. I would walk quietly through town, eating my handfuls of berries or sometimes a loaf of delicious bread if someone didn't take it out of my hand first... I survived through spite, and a desire to one day see my enemies die. Then suddenly one day a local seemed happy to see me, - "I'm glad to see you!" They said - and I realised I had finally made a friend. My best friend. 

Now I had someone to visit. I had someone to avoid when I had influenza (my enemies saw me more frequently, as it happens, and 16 souls were lost) and someone to share my confectionery creations with and the simple joy of gazing at the stars. Then I realised I could afford dogs, and I started to think about marriage and continuing my lineage, because the farm was doing OK and I had outlived my enemies. 

So I guess you could say I'm doing OK now, and I'm looking forward to seeing what the future holds and watching my kids grow up and begin their own journeys.

There are so many things that the game developers have done right I hate to say that I wouldn't recommend it, but the things that they did wrong are so glaring that it's frustrating.

First off, it's a beautiful game visually. The paper type graphics are really fun and overall make for a lovely asthetic. Occasionally the "thick outline" for things that you can gather isn't really thick enough but that's a small problem and I figured out what I could click and what I couldn't easily enough. Though watch out for the mushrooms, they're a little harder to spot sometimes. A minor issue at best. The seasonal changes of the environment are gorgeous.

The gameplay itself is where I have really mixed feelings and is ultimately why I can't recommend it. I love both the cozy game/farming style games, historical games, and survival games so I was super excited about this game when I first heard about it. Unfortunately there are some "quality of life" things that are super annoying like not being able to use three of an item to create dye because one of them is a gold star and the others are silver and bronze. It's not a big deal, you can stick the lower quality stuff in the fridge or somewhere to preserve them and stick the higher quality stuff in your bag to degrade but it's still an annoying aspect that gets even more annoying as you're desperately trying to craft things but can't because it takes two and you have one gold and one bronze item.

The second really big thing that frustrates me is that the game is HUGELY customizeable, they did such an amazing job of allowing people to play it the way they want to. I eventually turned off the fishing mini-game because I got tired of my keyboard feeling like it was going to break trying to follow the switchbacks on the fish that were so crazy. Where the frustration comes in is twofold, one, I get the desire to show support for the LGBT+ community but for a SURVIVAL style game, even in the cozy environment where survival is actually in part dependant on a. relationships and b. reproduction I was hugely disturbed to see that the game allows all the male characters to become pregnant. What frustrates me is that because reproduction is actually one of the survival functions of the game, being able to not only marry whoever you want but actually breed with whoever you want with no restrictions and no way to toggle it on and off actually turns that portion of the game SUPER easy. It's disappointing because one of the things they sell the game on is the relationships. If this were a fantasy game not advertised as a more historical game it wouldn't be a huge deal except that it STILL makes survival for the geneological side of things SUPER easy with no way to increase the difficulty.

Apparently it's fine to actually destroy the total social and physical function of women's bodies by making every animal male and still able to reproduce (Yes, I checked and so far have yet to see the female sign next to the animals ever). Again, if you want to make a game that totally destroys and makes invisible one half the species, that's up to you, but it ruins the survival aspect of the game because it doesn't matter if I kill them all off indiscriminately. So long as I have two animals of the same type, food, and space, they'll just keep impregnating each other and producing. This is a survival game, having male and female with their distinct characteristics mean that you are forced to actually look at that side of animal husbandry and not accidentally kill off the females or you don't get eggs OR progeny. I would love for this and the romantic relationships for people to be changed so there is the option for easy mode (gaytopia where everyone gets pregnant) or hard mode (biological reality).

They also really missed a goldmine of opportunity by not adding in the historical representation and attitudes surrounding Christianity. Instead the only religion is witchcraft and there is zero alternative except to engage with it because it's either miss out on huge content in the game or jump in and become a witch. Again, not something that by itself is bad, I get it's a game, but it's a game predicated on history that prides itself on that apsect, but then throws it out the window to portray that history in a light the developers prefer. The worst part of this is it takes a game that's trying very hard for inclusivity and tells people, "You're included unless you're not like me", which defeats the whole point of "inclusion" meaning everybody. When you go join the coven you're told to keep it quiet because there are people who don't like their witchcraft but there's actually zero option for anything else. There's a graveyard with a little masoleum in it with no indications that it's anything else but any reference to Christianity which was the prevelant religion at the time isn't there. It would be way more interesting from a survival side of things if the game had the church in it as an option with equivelent medicines and miracles as the witch's magic. Again, the game has mermaids so I know they're not really keeping to historical accuracy, but I think it would have been amazing.

Finally the travel distances. The village is HUGE. It can literally take you all day to walk from one end to the other. There are magic potions and stuff that can cut that down, sure, no problem there, but it feels like some of the distances are purely to ensure that you have to engage in the magic side of things. Not a problem but just seems like a time waster. Especially since the rewards for walking around the whole map and collecting resources are generally quite small. The mines drop very little ore for how long it takes to get there. It's beautiful but it gets super repetative very quickly.

Same with the relationships. If you just chat with everyone you meet along the way and show up for the market on sunday it's not really hard to build the relationships. There's very little interaction really and your spouse/family are useful if they're apprenticed somewhere handy, but it would be nice if making them a "farm helper" didn't totally tank their prospects until they move out of your house. For a game based on the social aspect it's surprisingly thin.

My HOPE is that if you play long enough from the 1700s then eventually you'll get to throw tea in the harbor, but I'm thinking that with how little actual story they've put into their game they probably haven't prepared things that far in advance, BUT I hope I'm wrong or that they add it in as late game content. Otherwise it's a very thin farming sim with some vaguely survivial-esque aspects (if you've ever played hardcore survival games this is very easy though the usual cozy youtubers that I'm watching are having a hard time with it so I guess it's not for people like me who enjoy both).

They do so many things well, but they could improve it substantially by getting a writer in (I'm available for longterm and character development if you're interested Devs) who knows how to create longterm and intricate stories that still allow players to play the game they want to play. I'm curious to hit my second generation after my first to see if taxes reset or not.

Overall it's a game that still has a lot of potential and is okay on it's own, but I wouldn't recommend it at this moment unless you're looking for a fairly flat game with a slightly interesting twist that doesn't quite allow you to take it all the way.

This game feels very half-baked...
Don't get me wrong, it delivers on everything it promises, but everything is just so... meh.

Let's start with the good stuff:
- Music is amazing!
- Graphics style is interesting - looks like inspired from Don't Starve or Paper Mario
- Options for making the game easier
- Good variety of crops, tools, decor items and ingredients
- Good amount of avatar customisation

The meh:
- There is no real story. Not that this type of game needs one, but this game is barely even trying.
- The villagers are extremely generic. I assume, that's because they are meant to age and die, and get replaced, but it also makes it much harder to get attached to anyone. After playing for a few evenings, I would recognise ~3 characters by their looks, but I know the name of none. Also, why is there an option to insult them? Why would I ever want to click that?!
- The camera perspective is way too shallow for the world. I appreciate the attempt at "flat" 2d mixed with 3d, but it just doesn't work if big parts of each set are behind the camera. You need to walk all the way in the direction of the camera to get a good overview of any place. Also, on the farm, the trees in front of the camera are very annoying. The whole problem could be solved by either placing the camera a bit higher and looking down at a steeper angle, or making the places more left-right heavy, without relying too much on depth.

The bad:
- The tools. Who thought it was a good idea that you just buy all the best tools? Not that it matters much, because for the most part, they are identical and only get used up slower. It's also very frustrating when you don't realise that you only had one charge left, because now you broke your tool that you could have had repaired for half the price of a new one.
- The farming. Watering crops in this game is a nightmare. There is not a single improvement! No irrigation ditches, better watering cans, nothing! Only an item that summons rain, but it's impossible to get regularly. This is a farming game and the farming aspect is absolutely braindead grindy because of the lack of any automation. I assume you'll be able to hire farm hands or ask your family to help out with the farm, but in my and my partner's playthroughs we did not get anywhere close to that within multiple days of playing.

I wanted to love this game so much.

And at first, I did. My first few hours in the game were pretty nice, but certain issues became apparent with more playtime. The love and work the Devs put in are clear to see, and I'm sure lots of people will have a great time with this. But for me many of the features that set Plum Grove apart also harm it in the end.

The generational gameplay loop, the fact that NPCs can marry, die, etc. It made you think the town and world would feel alive, but that's what killed it in my opinion. The NPC interaction is so shallow and lifeless, so meaningless ultimately. As an old timer of the farm/life sim genre, I know you rarely get novel-level character development, but this was so much less than even what Harvest Moon had on the SNES. 

The NPC weddings that come and go throughout the seasons feel like nothing more than a game of random ''pair the spares'' since no one really has any relationships with each other. No rival events, no dialogue hinting at who they might be interested in. It all feels so pointless, that not even the deaths shake you that much, most of them you never really even know by name anyway.

Even your own marriage is a dull affair. Again no relationship events, no special dialogue, nothing. All the NPCs are basically just randomly generated sims meant to keep the wheelwork of the generations going. In essence, in order to have a game where infinite generations were possible it made none of them matter. 

I could add that the economy is sort of broken besides. As crops are almost so worthless I nearly stopped growing them apart from a few to eat. But I realize that could get sorted out with tweaking and such.

Overall, I love the art and I respect the dedication of the Devs, but please consider what you want out of the game before you buy.

This game is ambitious as all hell, but it fails to deliver a bit in my opinion. First the pros:
-Excellent Graphics: very reminiscent of Paper Mario in the best way possible
-Fresh Premise: the idea of playing as your character's next of kin is VERY interesting
-A Few Welcome QoL things: Fast travel right off the bat, very customizable difficulty, not forced to pass out at 2AM

And then we come to the cons, and while there may be more later on in the game I don't know about these are the two I personally dealt with:
-It's very easy to move too soon and cancel your interactions (watering, picking things up, etc.) 
-By the nature of the system, it would be a TREMENDOUS (almost unthinkable) amount of effort to write interesting characters and dialogue for every character, as this is a multi-generational story with no guarantee that most of the characters you would have to write for will even be born in any particular game. This, unfortunately, leads to a lot of repetitious and procedural speech with very little to distinguish any of the characters besides their job and their physical description. This also bleeds into the quest system, which is, again, pretty much required to be able to give you any quest from any person on the list of possible townsfolk. I had 4 villagers send me a quest in the mail for a Pawpaw Fruit in first 4 days of being off my tutorial leash (which has its own problems, but I won't whine about how fast Pawpaw fruit rot as that's something you can customize in the difficulty settings) 

I'm willing to own the fact that I only played about 4 hours of this game, so some of my gripes might be addressed by later elements I didn't get to, but the fact of the matter is that I quickly came to feel like I was the only person in Plum Grove and I couldn't remember any of the character's names even a minute after meeting them. I'll be interested to see if something changes, because I REALLY want to like this one, but for now it's got to be a pass on this one from me.

[h1] The Plum Still Needs Time to Grow [/h1]

[b] What I Liked [/b]

The art style is one of the most endearing parts of the game.  It's a blatant Paper Mario look, but it works well for this type of game.

[b] What I Did Not Like [/b]

I don't want to say I disliked everything else - I don't.  It's just all half baked.  This game is an early access title in all but name only.  In combing the discussion points, there are bunch of posts about features that the developer intends to add.  Some assets are in the game - they just don't do anything yet.

The items aren't clearly marked if they have a use.  I made a herb garden, thinking it would grow herbs automatically or something.  But it's just decoration.  Received a painting, but no way to place it on the wall.

The dialog is very basic as well.  I already click through talking to every NPC just to raise my social score.  Otherwise, I don't care about the NPCs unless I plan to marry one of them.  Even once married, not much flavor text is added.  My spouse may live with me, but they stand in the doorway most of the time.  The town doesn't feel as alive as compared to other games of a similar nature.

It was also very quick to marry someone and have a child.  Sure, I can take it slow, but it would be boring since there isn't much depth in the NPC's.  My wife called me dear and said it was great being with me, but I had no attachment to her as compared to other games where I had a partner I could be with.  There was no depth to her except that she drank a bit and liked fishing.  It almost felt like dialog written by AI (not accusing the developer of that, just saying what it felt like).

[b] Why I Stopped Playing [/b]

I stopped because it's an early access title.  I bet in a couple years it'll be a great game.  For now, there are games out there that do this better.

Right now the game is a sapling.  In a couple years, I bet it'll be a tree.  I expect a great one.

[b] To address some comments: [/b]

1.  It's only made by two devs.  Okay, and?  Why do we keep justifying issues with a product by how many work on it?  I paid for the product, I'll provide my feedback.  The number of people working on it shouldn't impact a review.  If it was just two people, maybe it should have been early access.

2.  What other games do I recommend?  Sun Haven and Stardew Valley.

[b] Disclaimer [/b]

I have been a gamer for over 30 years.  I tend to play mostly PC games.  I also bounce around between games A LOT.  I may purchase a $60 game and play it for 2 hours or spend $10 on a game and spend 50 hours on it.  Even if I played a game a short time, it does not mean it is bad.  It just means another game caught my attention.  I also complain about flaws in games a lot, even about the littlest of things.  Keep that in mind when reading my reviews.  If I do not have a complaint, then the game must be special!

I was eager to fall in love with Echoes of the Plum Grove, but alas, it's all grind and no soul. Here's the lowdown on what's missing:

1. Farming Frustrations: The lack of an irrigation system means you'll spend half your day watering crops until you finally recruit a helper. But even then, it's a chore to keep their watering can filled.

2. Scarce Stones: Despite ample land and access to caves, finding basic resources like stone is a headache. Gems and ore? Sure. But a simple stone? Good luck.

3. Resource Riddle: There's an abundance of items with no apparent purpose—at least not yet. Prepare to hoard and hope for the best.

4. Townie Troubles: The townsfolk lack depth, and their random, impersonal dialogue makes it hard to care about their fates. Don't expect enriching lore or meaningful events to spice up your interactions.

5. Familial Flatness: Family life is basic—no tending to them, just glorified housemates. The legacy system falls flat, offering little impact on gameplay.

6. Tedious Trekking: Navigating the town is a mind-numbing exercise in repetition. Even with fast travel, you'll spend endless hours walking the same paths, encountering the same static scenery day in, day out.

7. Mundane Mining: Mining is a slog of walking to the same spots every day. It's a snooze-fest.

8. Inventory Ineptitude: The lack of inventory upgrades or organization tools is criminal in a game centered on grinding. Tracking items is a headache—paging Stardew Valley and Coral Island for a lesson in inventory management.

9. Ghostly Gripes: Interacting with the deceased yields quests, but the rewards feel lackluster. Spending hours just to reach them hardly seems worth the effort.

10. Interaction and Mapping Mishaps: Actions aren't stacked, so clicking on something else during an action cancels it instead of stacking it. It's inconvenient and frustrating, especially since you're forced to use the trackpad instead of a more intuitive action button like 'E'.

In summary, Echoes of the Plum Grove falls short of its promise of fun and eventful gameplay. Even town events lack interactivity. It feels more like an early access title than a fully realized game. 

Here's hoping for substantial improvements in future updates—because as it stands, it's not worth your money,

**EDIT**

Just to clarify, I am choosing to not recommend this game because of the lack of content and the misleading marketing. I've been following the devs on TikTok and was really excited about its release, but this is not the legacy, eventful farming sim they hyped—it’s more of a survival game. 

I hate to bring other game titles into this, but think Don't Starve (note: in my original review, I referenced Stardew Valley and Coral Island only to highlight successful inventory systems, not to compare the overall gameplay). Regarding the lack of content, there's still so much yet to be added that this feels like an early release. It's great that they have a rich roadmap, but it comes at the expense of a shallow full release.

Finally, just as a personal opinion, for those who, like me, dislike grinding games, it’s worth noting that the world is incredibly static. You can't even chop trees outside your farm—you can only shake the same ones over and over. Every day feels the same, which makes the game all about the grind.

Thank you, and please take this kindly—my intention is not to attack but rather to be precise with my experience so others can make an informed decision when buying the game as it stands right now.

I would love to give this game a grey middle rating. I don't feel comfortable to give it a thumbs down. 

But does the game deserve it? In some aspects, absolutely not, because the approach is wonderful and in many ways fantastically realised.

Let me explain. 

Echoes of the Plum Grove starts off very strong and is not only convincing in its interpersonal and perhaps even somewhat reprehensible possibilities, but also with its unique and beautiful graphics. I didn't find any bugs during my time playing and there were only a few very brief moments where I was thrown out of the immersion of the game.

So why do I feel unable to give this game a thumbs up?

1. the game quickly reveals that it is primarily about the people who live in the village of Honeywood. While the interactions with the inhabitants are very varied and coherent, the possibility of a romance, which is marketed here on Steam as a possible "inheritance", is ... just not good and lacks many things. The possible scenes and interactions with the beloved and later spouses are so life- and loveless and brief that I would hardly describe them as really existing. In fact, they don't exist at all.

Of course, one could argue about whether the game aims to be a romance simulator, and no, Echoes of the Plum Grove certainly doesn't, BUT if you provide the opportunity to start a romance and get married and have children, the interactions with the potential spouse, the future partner and also with the children should go beyond empty phrases and one-liners. 

Soon, you'll realise that there is a clear lack of attention to detail when said spouse and/or child simply stand in the same place in your house every evening and morning and stare blankly at the wall. Interactions are limited to "Here's some of the money I earned at work today" and that's almost it. And even if all these things are not a central motivation & mechanic for me to buy Echoes of the Plum Grove, it bothers me when opportunities are presented in a game, just to implement them so carelessly. 

If you commit to something, do it at least with some attention to detail. Put some care into it. 

The weddings and funerals, which in my opinion take place in a more or less random sequence, breathe a lot of life into everyday life in Honeywood... and, in my opinion, this is sorely needed. However, as it's always the same scene without dialoge, I lacked motivation to take part in these gatherings from summer onwards. If you see the same scene 5 times, you just won't do another 50. 

And that is a symptom throughout the whole game.

As in other farming simulators, Echoes of the Plum Grove also aims to make life in Honeywood more varied by incorporating festivals, such as a fishing or cooking festival. Unfortunately, even these festivals lack the necessary explanation or depth to be attractive, fun or meaningful in any way.

Overall, this shows me that Echoes of the Plum Grove, with its focus on the inhabitants of the village and the interpersonal system, is a great concept with a beautiful setting, but has not even begun to exploit its full potential.

2. the world of Echoes of the Plum Grove is small. My thesis is that they tried to compensate a bit by making the character's general movement speed a bit slower and offering several teleportation points instead, but still, by the start of fall in my playthrough at the latest, I noticed that the game simply doesn't has much to offer in its world and is quickly exhausted in its possibilities. 

Right from the start of the game, as in other famous farming simulators, you realize that you have the option, to use collected materials to repair a destroyed bridge in order to gain access to a previously unfamiliar location—but said location turns out to be a small section of the beach that exists solely to continue the main quest ONCE. Although pretty to look at, this place has little to no added value and is therefore not an argument for me to see the world as a little less confining due to its size.

3. and not only the character interactions and possibilities with the romances, spouses, children as well as the world size is small, but also the mine shown in the game. 

Like many other farming simulators, Echoes of the Plum Grove did not miss the opportunity to implement a mine where you can farm ores. I don't want to say too much, except that the mine gives me the impression of a Sims game, where the written stories are more "imagine and pretend" than actually presented mechanics. 

In no game have I found such a ridiculous mine, which is even more demotivating to visit because the descent to said farmable gems takes significantly longer than mining the gems themselves. Said stones can be counted on one hand and are always found in the same places.

Farming in Echoes of the Plum Grove is nothing but tedious and slow, which could be fitting to the survival-aspect of the game and its harsh approach on realism, death and "the old times", but considering it also wanting to be a storytelling farming-simulator, these concepts just do not sit well together. 

I just can't find the motivation to grind for wood by slowly walking across the map, shaking trees every day. It is always the same. It doesn't feel motivating or rewarding in way.

4 [CONTAINS SLIGHT SPOILERS!]
The main quest finally leads us to the witch and what lies hidden beneath her house. Even if this reveal seems really creative at first and rekindles curiosity about the game and its story, this euphoria quickly fell flat again for me. 

As in other farming simulators, what we find is what the community house was in Stardew Valley. 
Is it just as motivating as the many competing games? Not in the slightest, because the pacing in Echoes of the Plum Grove is so much slower and differentiated that it is anything but pleasant to fulfil these tasks at all, in addition to the survival elements and correspondingly lengthy processes to get hold of some items. 


Summary:

What I’m trying to say is, that the game lacks longevity, variety, motivation and depth—which results in missing the one thing I’ve always loved about farming simulators: replayability.

Echoes of the Plum Grove is one of the few games on the market I really regret knowing it isn't an early access, because despite its remarkable optimization, it unfortunately feels rushed and lifeless behind the package. 

As I head towards fall in my playthrough, there's a feeling which becomes more and more overwhelming. A feeling that something is just... missing? There is a lack of long-term motivation. There is a lack of depth and there is a lack of challenge.

There's just the lack of everything, including the hope for "new things".

After getting used to the game and its pacing, its processes and its characters, witnessing the lackluster romance & marriage, the soulless children, I quickly felt that I lacked the motivation to continue at all.

And considering that Echoes of the Plum Grove is cross-generational, which is advertised as a big selling point of the game, I personally don't see myself beeing motivated enough to give it the needed attention in the long-term. I really wan't to, but there's just not enough to do in Echoes of the Plum Grove.

And that's such a shame.

Ok, here are the Pros: 

Adjustable difficulty level: You can turn on/off all the extras (needing to eat, diseases, aging, the fishing minigame, etc) not just at the beginning of the game, but anytime you want, which is nice. 

Shops: You trade with the actual shopkeepers - so if you get to the shop after hours, that's okay! Just find the shopkeeper, and they'll be willing to trade with you at any time. 

Scenery: I thought the artwork would "fall flat" for me, but I think they really pulled it off, and it turned out super cute. 

I also really like that you aren't forced to go to sleep at a certain time - if you want to stay up all night working, you can. 

And now we move on to the Cons: 

Characters: 
The character interactions are lifeless and boring. You can marry and have children, and even decorate their rooms for them in your home - but they stand in the corner and stare at the wall the entire time they're in the house, so they'll never see what you've done. 

Crafting Skills: 
Mining - The mine is 3 rooms, and each room has one mining spot in it. It takes more time to walk to the mine and get to the mining spots than it does to clear the entire mine. 

Farming - This is supposed to be a farming sim. Each season, there are 4 or 5 crops you can grow. But you aren't going to want to do that, because you have to literally hoe/plant/water ONE SQUARE AT A TIME, no matter if you buy the upgraded tools or not. And if you don't turn off the option in the settings, your tools break. There's no automation, no sprinklers, no nothing. So every single day you waste a ton of time trying to farm. If you have a family, you can force them to help, but a lot of the time, you have to really hold their hand through it and you can't trust them to get it done.

Foraging - You have an axe, but you can't chop down any trees in the forest. To get wood, you shake a tree once a day and 2 pieces of wood drop. That's how you get wood without having to purchase it from a villager. But the thing is, when you craft an item, or build a building (like upgrading your house, or building a barn/coop) you require about 398 bajillion wood. 

Cooking - They make cooking far more difficult than it needs to be by including some items in recipes that can only be found on the ground during one particular season and are super rare. I played through 2 years of the game just to make sure I gave it a fair shot, and found 1 singular fiddlehead fern and NEVER found a pawpaw fruit. 

Quests: 
All the quests are just fetch quests. There's no plot or storyline with the villagers - there IS a main storyline  in the game (kinda), but to complete it you just...do more fetch quests as you try to fill pillars (similar to Coral Island or SDV community center, if you've played those). 

Other annoying things that aren't really dealbreakers but still bother me: 
You move SO slowly, and there is no sprint. If it's dark, and you don't have a lantern filled with oil that also costs money, you move even slower. Which I'm guessing they did because they were hoping you wouldn't notice how small the map is. The seasonal events have zero explanations (a sign at the event, or even a letter in the mail explaining things would have been very beneficial) and are honestly pretty boring, because there's just one main event to accomplish, and then that's it. There's no real unique dialogue, no activities you can participate in with the other villagers, nothing. And honestly, one of the events is a crafting event, where you LEAVE THE EVENT to go home and craft your item. So it doesn't even feel like a special event!


It's like they knew their game didn't have a lot of substance, so they made sure that everything you did was incredibly time consuming, so you wouldn't realize that your hours of gameplay were being taken up with things like fetching another lost toy, or planting one singular crop at a time.  And I honestly hate that, because the concept of this game was pretty neat, and I was really excited about it. Combining a cozy farm simulator with a life sim where you have to worry about keeping your villagers alive, and making it through a rough Winter, and making sure everyone has enough food and doesn't die of disease - I thought it was an awesome idea. Unfortunately, in this case, it just fell flat. There is no replayability for me - I was so bored before even the end of year one that trying to make my way through year two was a real slog. With a game like this, not wanting to continue to play defeats the entire purpose of the whole "continuing gameplay as your ancestors" idea. Anyway, for me, this game falls as flat as the trees I have to shake every day.

Positives first: the devs are engaged and eager to fix problems that come up.  The game is adorable (I hugged a bear!!).  The art is really great, the world is beautiful and the concept is intriguing.

The negatives: It becomes very grindy.  Some mechanics are simply not explained or not explained very well.  The game feels a little confused.  It's obviously set in colonial times but it's like one of those historical romance novels that say they're set in one time period but everyone is doing/saying/acting how people act in the present.  I never got the feeling that anything my character was doing was influencing anything else in the town.  My character dropped dead in the town square with several characters nearby and nobody even blinked.  Your character can emote (something that's not explained and I'm not sure I understand), but the NPCs don't seem to react to anything you do so it feels disjointed, like you should be part of the town but just aren't.  They also respond to each other in the same static way, comes off as stiff.  For example, if Mary keels over one day from the plague, there will be a funeral and no one will ever mention her again.  You could dance at the funeral and noone will notice and noone will ever mention it.  The NPCs just don't react naturally, by itself probably fine, but the whole idea here is that the town is living and breathing and reacting to your choices.  Example: my character has a baby and goes to talk to the husband.  Husband doesn't say anything about this significant life event.  He said the equivalent of "nice weather we're having".  Paying taxes for a town that never changes or grows or improves is a weird thing.  That tax thing, btw - you can opt out (again, something that's not well explained, because you have to select opting out on one option screen then navigate to another that has an oddly placed "apply" button and select to apply settings), but there is NO grace period if you don't pay your taxes on time.  There's really no way for you to buy recipes from a central location, like for food or building things, you have to come across them in a random shop or by trading with a random NPC or doing some tasks for a NPC.  Example: paint.  It's required for house upgrades.  The ONLY way I have found to buy paint is from the ships that come into port, but there is no way to obtain this info in the game unless you happen to go down to the port and try to trade with the captain of the ship.  The town is devoid of religion or religious symbols, but everyone is hung up on the witch who is practising magic (and I don't want to spoil anything but there are ghosts and afterlife components) which makes it the only religion in the game and makes religion strangely nondiverse.  The hunger/food relationship and economy really seem unbalanced.  

I enjoyed the first few hours, but after getting married and building a nicer house, I'm back to grinding away at trees which are strangely non-sustainable (at least the ones on the farm don't seem to regenerate) to make decent money.  I built a charcoal kiln and a smelter but can't figure out how to use the smelter and there's no guidance for it in-game. Update: I did figure out how to use them through trial and error.  It has led to less grinding, so that's good.

There's just too many things that feel arbitrary or not thought through and/or contradictory in this game for me to recommend it right now.  If you're ok with all these things, or them potentially not changing, then grab it because you'll love it.  I have high hopes that things will get ironed out and/or improved because the devs seem to love their game very very much and I wish the best for it.
